I really enjoyed *Aguirre* when I watched it a few months ago. The only Herzog films that I had seen were *Grizzly Man* and *Rescue Dawn*, so I didn't know what I was in for. 

I was awed by how Herzog showed us this lush landscape surrounding the characters and yet made the setting feel bleak. I was especially struck by the final scene. The roaring of the river and the sound of the monkeys as they overtake the raft. Aguirre asks, "Who else is with me," as we see a man left to his madness.

I really think it's a great film. It's got me interested to dive further into Herzog's filmography.

Absolutely love this one! I think of it as an entry into the "Heart of Darkness" microgenre (deeper into the jungle, deeper into self/madness, etc.). Definitely watch Fitzcarraldo now, also starring Kinski, for a slightly different take on the theme.

One of my favourite ever films. Kinski is legitimately terrifying and one of the greatest villains in cinema history in his role as Aguirre.

There's an oft asked question along the lines of *which is the best film with the smallest budget, ever made?*, and people point out things like Halloween or The Blair Witch Project, but when I'm asked it I always throw Aguirre into the mix. In today's money it was made for just over ~USD$2.5 million.

I highly recommend Werner Herzog's diary entries from the production and filming that were later adapted into a book. Also worth reading is the journals written during Fitzcarraldo which contain some incredible scenes with Kinski in a (different) rainforest. It's called *Scenarios: Aguirre, the Wrath of God; Every Man for Himself and God Against All; Land of Silence and Darkness; Fitzcarraldo*

It's difficult to recommend Herzog films because there are so many masterpieces, but if you're in the mood for Herzog just chilling out and talking about history/sociology/anthropology I highly recommend *Cave of Forgotten Dreams*.

I was blown away by the movie when I saw it. Kinda incredible that in order to film a madman conquistador going down rapids on rafts in the amazon, they hired a madman to dress in costume to get on a raft and go down rapids in the amazon. The commitment to the bit is the strength of the film. Also the music is dope with the opening scene.
The film for me is Apocalypse Now before Apocalypse Now even existed. Just like Apocalypse Now, the words "The horror, the horror" would perfectly describe this film. A masterpiece.

My hot take about this movie is that it is in some way the best movie about the ecological crisis : these "what are they even doing" absurd thing that the characters do, carrying their beautiful dresses, cannons, and horses in the middle of the jungle, claiming to conquer the whole region,  cannot but make me think about our societies wanting to carry on with our individual cars, transcontinental flights, etc..., thinking about conquering Mars, with the climate catastrophy looming

It was *Aguirre* that put me onto Werner Herzog about a year ago, and he's now hands down my favorite director. *Stroszek* is my favorite by him and it's gunning to be my #1 movie of all time, he has such a unique way of blending the completely absurd with grounded neorealism, even in his documentaries. The past 2ish months I've been trying to watch everything in his filmography and I think I'm up to 14 or 15 films, not a single one of them has been bad (some of them just OK). 

P.S you can stream almost all of his movies up until the 2000s for free with ads on the Shout Factory website if you're interested in watching them, that's how i've been doing it : [https://shout-tv.com/film/werner-herzog-film-collection](https://shout-tv.com/film/werner-herzog-film-collection)
I’ve seen revival houses do these as a double bill. A lot of madness on the river.

I'm pretty sure the book you're referencing at the end is called *Conquest of the Useless.* 

Also highly recommend his documentary *My Best Fiend* on the subject of his and Kinski's relationship.
You should watch Fitzcarraldo if you like commitment to the bit..

It's arguably Herzog's best film and work by Kinski. The opening scene alone is a marvel and def, something that wouldn't even be attempted today (because it's obviously dangerous and a huge liability lol). I first saw it on a whim after picking it up at the video store (remember those lol) and not knowing anything about it. When it was done, I must have sat there in stunned silence for ten min. It's just such incredible cinema!

The big three in Herzog's "Kinski going mad in harsh but beautiful landscapes" are this, Fitzcarraldo, and Cobra Verde. If you enjoyed Aguirre then I highly recommend both of those!

Burden of Dreams is also a great supplement to Fitzcarraldo after you've watched that.

Absurd? Sisyphean? Wait till you see Fitzcarraldo.

There's an insane quasi-doc he made about the burning oil fields of Kuwait from the first Gulf War. I won't spoil it but most of us never saw this kind of footage of the epic disaster and there's a particular moment that encapsulates the folly of human futility so darkly, you're going to want to watch it. It's definitely one of the themes running throughout his work. *Lessons Of Darkness* (1992)

it feels impossible from the start and never ever moves away from that, within minutes it’s doomed and i think i didn’t fully grasp that was the point on my initial watch. the annihilation of what supposedly matters and the lack of ever feeling calm, pride without worthiness, constant stress and disaster.

it’s hard to watch, not in its content, but in it’s off timed dubbing and lack of movement. didn’t really connect with any of it on its own and the experience itself is the real worthwhile point. still, it seems more interesting in the genuine trials and tribulations the cast and crew are placed in than the movie itself, which is really slow once the intro is complete. i agree about the sheer absurdity of the characters being there.

the continuation of colonialism and its constant striving for more through the use of Aguirre was very successful for me. it highlights just how twisted and long lasting the bonds between him and our real present day world are.

watched Lessons of Darkness this week and it absolutely blew me away. i agree whole heartedly with your comments on it. his greatest work of what I’ve seen.

Fitzcarraldo was far less successful or entrancing than Aguirre as a film for me, but definitely has that same wonderful absurdity.

To be sure this film is overwhelmed by Kinski – in a good way. He, both literally and metaphorically, capsizes the film. An irresistible and dangerous force, like Don Quixote on a speedball, it is never clear whether he is playing himself, Aguirre (whose nickname was El Loco), or indeed Werner Herzog. But Herzog must have the final word:

“Kinski always says the jungle is full of erotic elements. I don’t see it so much as erotic. I see it more full of obscenity – fornication, asphyxiation and struggling for survival.”

I think it is a master piece. I love all of Herzog’s work. Have you seen “my best fiend?” When Herzog speaks about wanting to strangle Klaus Kinsky who was having a tantrum in the middle of the Amazon?

Fitzcarraldo! Last year I started traveling in Peru and found myself in Iquitos and one hotel is called Fitzcarraldo! Little did I know that I was walking on the land where this master piece had been shot… very humbling… 🫶

Very weird experience, but great movie!

I've watched no similar movies. Fitzcarraldo is good, but personally not as great as Aguirre.

Yes, I've loved Herzog and Kinski ever since I first watched Aguirre and a bunch of their other collaborations at a Herzog festival in Berkeley back in the 1980s. I became totally obsessed with them. There's a great film about their relationship called My Best Fiend. 

Roger Ebert said, "As a meditation by a director on an actor, it is unique; most show-biz docs involve the ritual exchange of compliments. My Best Fiend is about two men who both wanted to be dominant, who both had all the answers, who were inseparably bound together in love and hate, and who created extraordinary work – while all the time each resented the other's contribution"
